title: QUIC RFC 9000 S17P1 Packet Number Encoding Completion
purpose: Describe the focused S17P1 closure for packet-number encoding width, post-ack range sufficiency, and out-of-order recovery proof.
design_summary: The packet construction seam uses a four-byte packet-number field for Initial, Handshake, 0-RTT, and protected 1-RTT packet builders. The focused proof exercises the full-width pre-ack Initial and Handshake behavior, the largest post-ack packet-number difference that remains safely representable by four bytes, and late arrival of earlier packets after later packets have already been opened.
data_and_state_considerations: Handshake and Initial packets share the coordinator handshake packet-number counter, while 0-RTT and 1-RTT packets use the application packet-number counter. The proof keeps those counters local to the coordinator and validates the opened packet bytes rather than widening the public API for packet-number administration.
edge_cases_and_constraints: The pre-ack proof reaches the maximum four-byte packet-number value for Initial packets.
The post-ack proof reaches the largest difference for which a four-byte packet-number range remains greater than twice the gap from the largest acknowledged packet.
The out-of-order proof opens a later maximum four-byte packet number before the preceding packet number and then recovers the earlier packet.
The negative proof removes a packet-number byte from a late protected packet and verifies that the packet cannot be opened.
risks: This slice does not implement adaptive packet-number length selection.
This slice does not claim full packet-number reconstruction for arbitrary reordered receive windows.
This slice does not claim hosted interop readiness.
This slice does not close deferred fuzz obligations for S17P1.

supplemental_sections.heading: Boundary
supplemental_sections.content: This design closes the focused generated S17P1 packet-number encoding proof tail for REQ-QUIC-RFC9000-S17P1-0002 through REQ-QUIC-RFC9000-0925. It does not claim adaptive packet-number encoding, public packet-number control APIs, hosted interop readiness, or closure of deferred fuzz obligations.
